questions.question: What does "information-theoretic security" mean for QKD?

options.text: The key's secrecy follows from physical law, independent of the eavesdropper's computing power
The key is encrypted with AES-256
The key is secure only against classical attackers
The key is hard to compute with today's computers

questions.framework: QKD security rests on quantum mechanics (no-cloning, measurement disturbance), not computational hardness — so it survives even a quantum computer, unlike RSA/ECC.

questions.question: In BB84, what physical principle prevents an eavesdropper from copying the quantum states undetected?

options.text: The no-cloning theorem plus measurement disturbance

questions.framework: An unknown quantum state cannot be copied (no-cloning), and any measurement to learn it disturbs it, raising the QBER — this is how Eve is detected.

questions.question: QBER stands for:
questions.framework: QBER = fraction of sifted bits where Bob's decoded bit disagrees with Alice's; it is the master security indicator.

questions.question: In the project's model, QBER is computed as:

options.text: P_error / P_sift, where P_error = ½(P10 + P01) and P_sift includes all four detection outcomes

questions.framework: `sikd_performance.compute_Psift_QBER`: QBER = Perror/Psift, Perror = ½(P10+P01), Psift = ½(P00+P11+P10+P01).

questions.question: The Shor-Preskill / GLLP asymptotic secret key rate used here is:
questions.framework: `compute_SKR`: mutual info I(A;B)=1−H₂(Q), minus reconciliation leakage f_EC·H₂(Q), minus Eve's Holevo χ_E.

questions.question: At what QBER does the corrected SKR formula reach zero (for f_EC = 1, χ_E = 0)?
questions.framework: 1 − 2·H₂(Q) = 0 at Q ≈ 0.11 — the classic BB84 Shor-Preskill threshold; this is exactly why the EC-leakage term had to be added.

questions.question: Why was the earlier SKR formula (missing the reconciliation term) wrong?

options.text: It used the wrong entropy base
It reached zero only at QBER = 50%, contradicting the project's own "SKR = 0 above 11%" claim

questions.framework: Slepian-Wolf/Devetak-Winter: error correction leaks f_EC·H₂(Q) bits publicly even with no eavesdropper, so it must be subtracted.

questions.question: In the baseline analysis, χ_E (Eve's Holevo information) is set to:

options.text: 0 (no eavesdropping assumed for the performance baseline)

questions.framework: `compute_SKR(chi_E=0.0)`: performance is characterised assuming no active eavesdropper; χ_E > 0 would model an attack.

questions.question: H₂(p), the binary entropy, equals:
questions.framework: `binary_entropy`; returns 0 at p=0 or p=1; quantifies both mutual information and reconciliation cost.

questions.question: The mutual information I(A;B) between Alice and Bob is:
questions.framework: Binary symmetric channel capacity with crossover probability QBER; the raw information before subtracting leakage.

questions.question: Sifting in this dual-threshold scheme refers to:

options.text: Discarding samples that fall in the guard zone [d0, d1]

questions.framework: Samples inside [d0,d1] are ambiguous and discarded; P_sift is the probability a sample is confidently decoded as 0 or 1.

questions.question: The protocol whose noise model this project follows (Vu et al. 2022) actually implements:

options.text: BBM92 entanglement-based, with design target QBER ≤ 10⁻³

questions.framework: The provenance caveat — the noise/threshold machinery is borrowed from a BBM92 study; applying the BB84 11% bound is an explicit, stated assumption.

questions.question: After the v3 corrections (mₖ = 0.15), the QBER across 30°–90° elevation is:

options.text: Below ~0.02%, under even the stricter 10⁻³ BBM92 target

questions.framework: `IMPACT_EVALUATION.md`: the cross-talk /8 fix and mₖ→0.15 drop QBER far below threshold everywhere in the operating range.

questions.question: Privacy amplification (not explicitly coded here but implied by the SKR bound) serves to:

options.text: Compress the sifted key to remove any partial information Eve may hold

questions.framework: The χ_E term in the SKR bound is the amount removed by privacy amplification; secrecy is bought by shrinking the key.

questions.question: Why is 1550 nm chosen as the QKD carrier wavelength?

options.text: Telecom C-band: eye-safe, low fibre/atmosphere loss, mature components
It is the only wavelength lasers produce

questions.framework: System-parameter choice; 1550 nm also has weaker aerosol scattering than visible (Kruse/Kim exponent), aiding the link budget.

questions.framework: `compute_thresholds`; DT/DD is a CV-QKD-style continuous detection, which changes how daytime background noise matters.

options.text: Lower QBER (stronger key signal vs noise) and raise SKR, until the modulation budget binds

questions.question: The Holevo bound χ_E represents:

options.text: The maximum information Eve can hold about the key given her quantum side-information

questions.framework: Devetak-Winter secure rate = I(A;B) − χ_E; setting χ_E = 0 is the no-eavesdropper baseline.

questions.question: Why is a *composable* security proof listed as future work?

options.text: It removes the need for QKD
The current SKR is an asymptotic, non-composable bound that does not certify finite-key, trusted-relay end-to-end security

questions.framework: Leverrier (2015) composable CV-QKD; the trusted-relay XOR model needs a composable argument to be operationally secure end-to-end.

questions.question: In the trusted-relay key model, a satellite holding keys kA and kB for two stations broadcasts:

options.text: kA ⊕ kB (their bitwise XOR), so either ground node can recover the other's key

questions.framework: `schedulers` docstring; the pair's usable key is limited by the worse-served side, K_q = min(sideA, sideB).

questions.question: The security of the trusted-relay scheme fundamentally assumes:

options.text: The satellite node is trusted (not compromised)

questions.framework: "Trusted-relay" means the relay learns both keys; security holds only if the relay itself is honest — a known limitation of relay QKD.

questions.question: If QBER exceeds 11% on a pass, the correct interpretation is:

options.text: No positive secret key can be distilled on that pass (SKR = 0)

questions.framework: SKR bound goes non-positive; the pass yields raw bits but zero *secret* key.

questions.question: The reason cross-talk noise is uniquely a QKD concern (not just a classical-link concern) here is:

options.text: It raises QBER directly, and QBER caps the secret key by a steep entropy function

questions.framework: H₂(Q) rises sharply near threshold, so a small QBER increase from cross-talk can zero the secret key while barely denting classical BER.

questions.question: Gauss-Hermite quadrature is the natural choice for averaging over log-normal fading because:

options.text: In log-amplitude the variable is Gaussian, and GH quadrature integrates ∫e^(−x²)f(x)dx exactly for polynomials

questions.framework: X ~ N(−σ²_X, σ²_X); substitution ha = exp(2√(2σ²_X)x + 2μ_X) turns the fade average into the GH weight form.

questions.question: The single most important honesty point a QKD theorist should note about this thesis is:

options.text: It openly flags that the 11% BB84 threshold is borrowed from a BBM92-based model, an explicit assumption, not an inherited result

questions.framework: Provenance caveat in Ch. 6 — scientific integrity: state which claims are assumptions vs. validated inheritances.
